absent: Whether emergency remount reports or retries failures from context creation, data parsing, or super reconfiguration.
Ordering, exclusion, and sleeping rules for global super iteration beyond forward versus reverse traversal.
Meaning of freeze holder identities and nesting versus exclusive modifiers and required thaw matching.
Recovery and error values for device super insertion races beyond memory exhaustion and frozen busy.
Propagation of per super sync errors to global sync callers and emergency completion reporting.
Default values and write side effects for overflow user and group identity controls.
Path resolution truncation and failure handling for duplicate warnings and mount point removal errors.
Lifetime and ordering of backing objects and block sync relative to super shutdown.

findings.text: Emergency remount and emergency thaw-all provide asynchronous global recovery that allocates work state without sleeping and queues background iteration over all supers, each announcing completion through the kernel log.

Global freeze and thaw controls walk all supers in forward or reverse order and invoke filesystem specific freeze or thaw hooks with kernel holder identity when advertised, falling back to generic helpers otherwise.

Block backed super handling offers acquisition by device number, block file and backing configuration, mount tree construction with optional quiet device lookup, and teardown that syncs the block layer before releasing the holder file.

Block holder file lifecycle opens by device number or pathname with filesystem holder callbacks, records a per device super association that is refused while frozen, and later unregisters and releases the file.

Synchronization services flush inodes then filesystems then block devices, with background emergency variants that repeat the cycle and range helpers that stage early wait, write, and late wait phases in flag order.

Directory and mount point handling creates namespaced directories attached to their owners, supports removal, rename, and relocation across parents, and creates or deletes empty placeholder directories for mounts.
Writeback backing setup allocates and registers either a caller formatted per super object or a default uniquely sequenced one derived from filesystem type.

Small matching and delegation helpers compare supers by private data, unconditional acceptance, or device identity, initialize device numbers, prefer filesystem freeze hooks when present, and resolve owning objects, operations, and printable paths.
Active acquisition only succeeds when exclusive super protection can be taken and the active count can be raised from nonzero, always releasing the protection before returning the outcome.

Device keyed reuse rejects retired entries and requires device equality, while alternate matchers use private pointer equality or unconditional acceptance, and device setup stores the key before registration.

Freeze and thaw over one device preserve the first error for a lone filesystem but suppress errors when several supers share the device, with freeze additionally syncing the block device when no error remains.

Tree construction requires a source, disables security labelling, reuses an existing super only when read only state matches, otherwise configures block state, fills the super, marks it active, and pins its root.

Block super configuration refuses write access on read only devices and refuses mounts while the device freeze count is positive, then publishes block file, device, backing reference, stable write marking, identifier, debug name, and block size.
Global writeback helpers skip read only supers, and filesystem sync additionally skips supers marked to avoid sync or lacking a sync hook, using separate early and late passes.

Range synchronization rejects unknown flags, negative or wrapping offsets, clamps ranges beyond narrow page cache limits with zero length meaning to end, restricts object kinds, and performs waits and writes in flag order.

Freeze selection skips supers without any freeze capability, and partial power freeze further restricts to filesystems flagged for that mode, while thaw selection skips only those without freeze capability.

Directory creation fails on missing owner or parent, inherits the owner parent or falls back to the global root, applies owner identity to the new node, warns on collision, and records the node in the owner.
Device loss handling syncs unless surprise, shrinks cached names, evicts cached objects, and shuts down when no veto hook succeeds, while periodic device sync only acts on active rooted supers.

Emergency thaw callback holds an active reference, performs block level thaw without holding super write protection, then takes exclusive protection only for the locked thaw before dropping the reference.
Device holder callbacks release holder serialization before walking per device supers and acquire shared super protection or an active reference per entry, releasing after each step.

Freeze and thaw require filesystem freeze serialization on entry, use read side protection for device to super lookup, enforce an ordering barrier before sampling the freeze count, and serialize block binding updates with a global spinlock.

A dedicated spinlock serializes clearing of the owner node pointer against concurrent symlink target use, while file helpers use read side sections to reach the owner and assert node locking when flagged.
Per mount sync holds super read protection across the filesystem sync and then merges that outcome with advancement of the per file error sequence.
The filesystem holder operations table links four callbacks that handle device loss notification, device sync, device freeze, and device thaw for block devices claimed by filesystems.
The shared filesystem control table exposes two bounded integer entries for overflow user and group identity mapping with minimum and maximum limits.
Emergency remount visits only block backed writable supers and attempts a forced read only reconfiguration through a fresh context with empty monolithic data, always releasing the context afterwards.

Global sync moves from flusher wakeup through inode writeback, early filesystem sync, late filesystem sync, and early then late block sync, while emergency work interleaves repeated inode and filesystem passes with block sync.

Device super registration reuses a live entry when reference acquisition succeeds under read protection, otherwise allocates and inserts a new entry and then rechecks frozen state, rolling back with busy on a race.

System call entries provide whole system sync, per descriptor mount sync, full and data only object flush, and two range sync variants that forward to a shared range helper after descriptor validation.
Early initialization installs the shared filesystem control table under the filesystem namespace and reports success.
Asynchronous emergency paths do nothing when non sleeping work allocation fails, and device thaw retry loops continue until success while emitting a warning per attempt.
Duplicate names trigger a warning with resolved parent path and diagnostic dump, and removal checks directory type while tolerating an already cleared node.
Reuse that would flip read only state warns and fails busy instead of changing state, and frozen or read only block devices cause mount failure with a diagnostic message.
Freeze control combines kernel and userspace holder bits with nest and exclusive modifiers into holder and flag masks.
Range sync accepts a mask combining early wait, write, and late wait bits.
Overflow identity controls use owner writable world readable access, new directories use owner full with group and other read execute access, and diagnostic lines carry a fixed sysfs tag.
